title: The studio palette — and a finished reel
thesis: A new visual system built from her own room rather than from a campaign idea, and the first Reel this system has ever delivered as a finished file rather than a shot list. Seven posts: five colour-designed singles with no photograph in them at all, one educational carousel, and a 24-second cinematic MP4 she uploads as-is.
projection: Week 5's nine posts are the live experiment and the carousel result is not in yet, so this week deliberately changes only one variable — the look. The studio palette (fig green and clay, taken from the plants and timber in her own salon) replaces the marigold and the ticket rust, both of which were borrowed from campaign ideas rather than from the business. Target remains a return to the 6.19% account average with followers back to 182-184. The one thing to change: stop asking her to film and start handing her finished video, because three weeks of guides produced zero filmed reels and the constraint is her time, not her willingness. What this sets up for next week is the cleanest test the account has had — a finished Reel against a week of stills, with the same palette on both, so the medium question gets answered without design as a confound.

posts.title: Four things quietly wrecking your colour
posts.imageAlt: A 24-second vertical reel. It opens on glossy brunette waves with the line "This is what six weeks later should look like", then moves through four struck-through don'ts on deep ink with a rust marker, each answered by a photograph or a clay-coloured card, and closes on cream with the toner and gloss price and the Sunday hours.
posts.whyItWorks: Three weeks of video guides produced no filmed reels, which says the constraint is her time rather than her willingness — so this one arrives finished. The structure follows what the 2026 salon research puts first: open on the desired result rather than the before, then pair wrong against right instead of listing tips. The don'ts are struck through in rust on ink and the dos land on photographs and clay, so the rhythm is legible with the sound off, which is how most of the feed watches. Every frame was rendered as type rather than generated, so the price on the closing card is exact.

caption.hook: Four things quietly wrecking your colour, and none of them cost anything to fix.
caption.body:
Washing it the day you get home, when the cuticle is still open and everything you just paid for goes down the drain. Rinsing in hot water, which opens the cuticle again every single wash. Purple shampoo daily, when it is a toner and not a shampoo. And straightening on the highest heat, when 185 degrees is plenty on coloured hair.

None of these are a product you have to buy from me. They are just the four I explain most.
caption.cta: Save this for your next wash day. Toner and gloss is $45 and takes 45 minutes.

howToPost: Upload the MP4 as a reel. It is already 1080x1920 and about 24 seconds.

There is no audio on it on purpose — add a track in the app so you can pick something trending on the day. Try the trending list first; if a song will not attach, that is the account type, so take the next one.
Set w6-reel-cover.png as the cover if the app does not pick the first frame.
Ask for the save in your first comment. This one is built to be saved and sent.

posts.title: Hair you stop thinking about
posts.imageAlt: A deep fig-green card with a clay disc in the top corner. Large serif type reads "Hair you stop thinking about", with a paragraph beneath about colour built to grow out rather than to photograph well once.
posts.whyItWorks: This is the post the operator asked for — it shows what is wanted rather than what was done. There is no photograph of finished hair on it and it is still unmistakably about hair, which is the point: the promise is a feeling, not a result someone else got. It also quietly positions against the entire local market, because every other salon in Camberwell is posting the photograph. The line about growing out rather than photographing well once is her actual specialism stated as a value rather than a service.

caption.hook: The brief is not really a colour. It is hair you stop thinking about.
caption.body:
Most people do not want to be thrilled with their hair for four days and anxious about it for six weeks. They want to stop noticing it.

That is a different job to making it look good in the chair. It means shadowing the root so the grow-out is soft, picking a tone that fades to something you can live with, and being honest about how often you will realistically get back in.
caption.cta: If that is what you are after, DM me and tell me how often you can come in. I will build it around that.

howToPost: Tuesday morning. This is the week's tone-setter and carries no offer.
If anyone replies about their own grow-out, answer publicly. It is what makes the next person ask.

posts.title: Five ways to be blonde
posts.imageAlt: A cream card headed "Five ways to be blonde", listing Lived-in, Buttery, Icy, Babylit and Grown-out, each with a short description. A footer reads From $240 and DM for yours.
posts.whyItWorks: Naming the options is what lets someone want a specific one. Most clients arrive asking for blonde and leave with whatever the colourist heard, and the gap between those two is where disappointment lives. Giving the five a vocabulary makes the consultation shorter and the expectation sharper, and it does price anchoring with a single From figure rather than a list. It is also the most saveable thing in the week — someone screenshots this and brings it back in November.

caption.hook: Blonde is not one thing, and asking for it as one thing is how people end up with a colour they did not mean.
caption.body:
Lived-in is soft and hand-painted with no regrowth line, for anyone who cannot get back often. Buttery is warm rather than icy and is kindest on darker natural hair. Icy is the brightest and the highest maintenance of the five. Babylit is very fine foils close to the root, the most natural and the slowest to do. Grown-out is deliberately shadowed so it is still beautiful at week twelve.

Pick the one that matches your diary, not the one that matches the photo.
caption.cta: Save this, then DM me which one sounds like yours

howToPost: Wednesday morning. Wednesday and Thursday are still the quiet days, so this one earns its slot by starting conversations that fill them.
Ask for the save in the first comment, not the caption.

posts.title: Four things quietly wrecking your colour — the carousel
posts.imageAlt: Five-slide carousel in the studio palette. A clay cover, three ink slides each carrying a struck-through don't in rust, and a cream closing slide about straightening heat and the toner and gloss price.
posts.whyItWorks: The same content as Monday's reel, in the format the feed reads differently — which makes this the cleanest experiment the account has run. Identical words, identical palette, one as video and one as a carousel, three days apart. Whatever the gap turns out to be is the medium effect with design held constant, and that is the question four weeks of data has been circling without ever isolating.

caption.hook: The four things I explain most, and none of them cost anything to fix.
caption.body:
Swipe through. Washing it too soon, rinsing too hot, purple shampoo too often, and the straightener too high.

If you only change one, change the water temperature. It is free and it is the one that makes the most difference to how long your tone lasts.
caption.cta: Save it for your next wash day

howToPost: All five slides in order, cream one last.
Post it Thursday even though Monday's reel says the same thing. That gap is the experiment — same words, same palette, different format.

posts.title: Twenty years of knowing when to stop
posts.imageAlt: A clay-coloured card with a fig-green disc in the top corner. Serif type reads "Twenty years of knowing when to stop", with a paragraph about the judgement being the thing you pay for.
posts.whyItWorks: It answers the price objection without naming a price, which is the only way to answer it without sounding defensive. Anyone can apply lightener; the expertise is the decision to stop, and stating that plainly reframes a four-hour appointment as judgement rather than labour. It also does the quiet work of pre-selling the honest no — a client who has read this is far less likely to push for three levels of lift in one sitting.

caption.hook: Anyone can put lightener on hair. That is not the part you are paying for.
caption.body:
The part you are paying for is someone watching it, deciding it has gone far enough, and being willing to say so out loud even when you were hoping for one shade lighter.

Twenty years is not twenty years of getting faster. It is twenty years of knowing what hair does about ten minutes before it does it.
caption.cta: Wednesday and Thursday are the quiet days this week. DM me if you want one.

howToPost: This is a good one to keep on your profile. Consider saving it to a highlight.

posts.title: Sundays, now open
posts.imageAlt: A fig-green card with a clay disc. The word SUN in clay outline above DAYS in solid cream, with 10 to 2 every Sunday beneath, and a clay button reading DM me the word Sunday.
posts.whyItWorks: The Sunday campaign look the operator liked, rebuilt on the studio palette so the announcement still reads as the same idea while the feed moves forward. Saturday morning is the right slot because it is when the weekend is already in someone's head and tomorrow is a real option rather than an abstraction. The scarcity is a timetable rather than a claim, so it holds up without a discount.

caption.hook: Sundays are open now, and there is exactly one chair.
caption.body:
Ten til two, every week. Four hours, one appointment, nobody else in the room.

It holds one big colour or a couple of smaller things, and that is the whole day. If a weekday has never worked for you, this is the one that might.
caption.cta: DM me the word Sunday and I will hold it

howToPost: Saturday morning, when tomorrow is a real option.
Put it on your story with the countdown sticker set to Sunday 10am.

posts.title: One chair. Ten til two.
posts.imageAlt: An ink card with a fig-green disc. Serif type reads "One chair. Ten til two." with a line about four hours holding one big colour, dated Sunday 20 September.
posts.whyItWorks: Sunday evening is when the coming week gets planned, so this posts the moment today's Sunday finishes and points straight at the next one. Closing the loop publicly matters more than the post itself — if today's chair was taken, saying so is what makes next week's scarcity believable rather than rhetorical.

caption.hook: One chair, ten til two, and it goes to whoever asks first.
caption.body:
Next Sunday is open. Four hours holds one big colour, so when it is taken the one after that is a week away.

If you have been putting something off because you could never find the time in the week, this is the time.

howToPost: Sunday about 5pm, as today's appointment finishes.
If today's Sunday was booked, say so on your story. A visibly gone appointment is what makes the next one believable.
